lesson_scope: Raising and hauling objects vertically and along inclined planes against gravity and resistance; calculation of gravitational potential energy changes (mgh); calculation of work done against friction and resistance forces; power and rate of doing work during hauling; multi-stage motion with acceleration and steady speed; work-energy theorem reconciliation.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 1: Vertical raising of a load at constant speed

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 1: Vertical raising of a load at constant speed

hints: At constant speed without resistance, the crane tension balances the weight of the load: $T = mg$.
Calculate work done using $W = mgh = 240 \times 10 \times 15 = 36000\text{ J}$.

walkthrough.text:
Identify the lifting tension required to raise the mass at constant speed:
$$T = mg = (240)(10) = 2400\text{ N}$$
The crane applies an upward force of $2400\text{ N}$.

Calculate the work done through the vertical displacement $h = 15\text{ m}$:
$$W = Th = (2400)(15) = 36000\text{ J}$$
The crane transfers $36000\text{ J}$ of energy to gravitational potential energy.

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Balance the vertical forces:
- Lifting at constant speed means acceleration is zero:
$$T = mg = 240 \times 10 = 2400\text{ N}$$
The cable supports the entire weight directly.

Compute total work done:
- Multiplying force by vertical height gives:
$$W = 2400 \times 15 = 36000\text{ J}$$
The crane does $36000\text{ J}$ of work raising the load.

ai_rubric.observable: Applies $W = mgh$ with $m = 240$, $g = 10$, and $h = 15$.
Obtains work done $W = 36000\text{ J}$ (or $36\text{ kJ}$).

walkthrough.text:

$$W = Th = (375)(12) = 4500\text{ J}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:

$$T = mg + R = 350 + 25 = 375\text{ N}$$
The tension must exceed weight by $25\text{ N}$.

Calculate the work done:
- Multiplying tension by the $12\text{ m}$ climb:
$$W = 375 \times 12 = 4500\text{ J}$$
$4200\text{ J}$ becomes potential energy and $300\text{ J}$ is lost to air resistance.

$$W = 300 \times 20 = 6000\text{ J}$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 4: Work done against friction along an inclined plane

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 4: Work done against friction along an inclined plane

hints: Work done against friction along a plane is simply the frictional force multiplied by the distance moved along the plane.

walkthrough.text:

$$W_{\text{fric}} = (32)(16) = 512\text{ J}$$

- Friction acts continuously along the $16\text{ m}$ slope:
$$F_r = 32\text{ N},\quad d = 16\text{ m}$$

Compute energy lost to friction:
- Multiplying resistance by path length gives:
$$W_{\text{fric}} = 32 \times 16 = 512\text{ J}$$
$512\text{ J}$ of energy is dissipated as heat against friction.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 5: Calculating pulling force for hauling on a rough slope at constant speed

hints: At constant speed, acceleration is zero, so the pulling force balances both the component of weight down the plane and friction.
Calculate $P = 400\sin 18^\circ + 50 \approx 123.61 + 50 = 173.61\text{ N} \approx 174\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Resolve forces parallel to the plane in equilibrium ($a = 0$):
$$\Sigma F_{\parallel} = 0 \implies P - mg\sin 18^\circ - F_r = 0$$
$$P = mg\sin 18^\circ + F_r$$

Substitute numerical values and solve for $P$:
$$P = (40)(10)\sin 18^\circ + 50 = 400\sin 18^\circ + 50$$
$$P \approx 123.607 + 50 = 173.607\text{ N} \approx 174\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Identify the forces resisting the haul:
- Weight pulling down the slope:
$$W_{\parallel} = mg\sin 18^\circ = 400\sin 18^\circ \approx 123.61\text{ N}$$
- Friction opposing the upward motion: $F_r = 50\text{ N}$.

Sum the opposing forces:
- The pulling force must overcome both:
$$P = 123.61 + 50 = 173.61\text{ N} \approx 174\text{ N}$$
The required pulling tension is $174\text{ N}$.

ai_rubric.observable: Resolves forces along the slope to form $P = mg\sin 18^\circ + F_r = 400\sin 18^\circ + 50$.
Obtains pulling force $P = 174\text{ N}$ (or $173.6\text{ N}$).

Set up the perpendicular force balance:
- The cable pulls upward away from the slope with $T\sin 18^\circ$:
$$R + T\sin 18^\circ = 450\cos 12^\circ \implies R = 450\cos 12^\circ - T\sin 18^\circ$$
The normal reaction is reduced by the upward cable component.

Form the parallel equation of equilibrium:
- The parallel pulling component balances component of weight and friction:
$$T\cos 18^\circ = 450\sin 12^\circ + 0.2 R$$
- Substituting the expression for $R$ yields the complete relation for $T$.

hints: During descent at constant speed, the component of gravity down the slope balances the upward cable tension plus resistance: $mg\sin 35^\circ = T + R_{\text{resist}}$.
Calculate $T = 12000\sin 35^\circ - 800 \approx 6882.88 - 800 = 6082.88\text{ N} \approx 6080\text{ N}$.
Because tension acts up the slope while displacement is down the slope, work done by tension is negative: $W_T = -(6082.88)(45) \approx -274000\text{ J}$.
State the work done by the tension as $-274000\text{ J}$ (or state that the work done against the tension is $274000\text{ J}$ or $274\text{ kJ}$).

Resolve forces parallel to the inclined track during steady descent ($a = 0$):
$$\Sigma F_{\parallel} = 0 \implies mg\sin 35^\circ - T - R_{\text{resist}} = 0$$
$$T = mg\sin 35^\circ - R_{\text{resist}}$$

Calculate the numerical value of the tension $T$:
$$T = (1200)(10)\sin 35^\circ - 800 = 12000\sin 35^\circ - 800$$
$$T \approx 6882.88 - 800 = 6082.88\text{ N} \approx 6080\text{ N}$$

Calculate the work done by the tension force over $d = 45\text{ m}$:
$$W_T = Td\cos 180^\circ = -(6082.88)(45) = -273729.6\text{ J} \approx -274000\text{ J} \quad (-274\text{ kJ})$$
The cable does $-274\text{ kJ}$ of work (or $274\text{ kJ}$ of work is done against the tension).

$$T = 6882.88 - 800 = 6082.88\text{ N} \approx 6080\text{ N}$$
The cable restrains the descent with $6080\text{ N}$.

$$9300 - 6882.88 = 2417.12\text{ N} = 1200a$$
$$a = \frac{2417.12}{1200} \approx 2.01425\text{ m s}^{-2} \approx 2.01\text{ m s}^{-2}$$

$$0 = 3^2 - 2(2.01425)s = 9 - 4.0285s$$
$$s = \frac{9}{4.0285} \approx 2.23409\text{ m} \approx 2.23\text{ m}$$

Calculate the work done by gravity during this braking descent:
$$W_g = (mg\sin 35^\circ)s = (6882.88)(2.23409) \approx 15376.9\text{ J} \approx 15400\text{ J} \quad (15.4\text{ kJ})$$
